title: Inverting the Script Probability
takeaway: To score how Arabic-like a string is, the paper needs $P(s|\text{Arabic})$, which would otherwise require a generative model of Arabic text. Bayes' rule replaces it with three quantities that are cheap to compute: a character-level script check, a unigram probability, and the corpus rate of Arabic script. The same construction is reused for Hebrew and any other script with its own Unicode blocks.
walkthrough:
This is one unnumbered line of algebra in the appendix, printed without a caption. It supplies one ingredient of the paper's [[computational-proxy]] for Arabic script.

### Why this quantity is needed

Every proxy in the paper has the same shape, a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) / P(s))$. It asks how much more likely a string $s$ is under the hypothesis "this is Arabic script" than under the corpus in general.

The denominator is easy. $P(s)$ is the [[unigram-p-s-estimate]] — multiply the frequency of each token in $s$.

The numerator is the awkward one. Writing $P(s|\text{Arabic})$ directly would mean building a generative model of Arabic text.

### How to read the line

Read it right to left. $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ runs the conditioning the other way: given the string, is it Arabic script? That is a classification question, and characters answer it.

Each of the three right-hand terms is cheap. $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ is set by checking whether every character of $s$ sits in an Arabic Unicode block, such as U+0600–U+06FF or U+0750–U+077F. All Arabic gives $1$; any character outside those blocks gives $10^{-10}$, a tiny value rather than a hard zero.

$P(s)$ is the unigram estimate again. $P(\text{Arabic})$ is measured by running the same character heuristic over a random sample of the dataset.

### What it buys

Substitute the line into the proxy and the unigram term cancels: $\log(P(\text{Arabic}|s)/P(\text{Arabic}))$. The score becomes a script check divided by the base rate of that script, and since Arabic is around $0.13\%$ of training tokens, a confidently-Arabic string scores high.

Two wrinkles. A token that is not a complete Unicode character — common, because [[utf8-multi-token-characters]] split across byte tokens — gets its script share estimated by sampling random occurrences instead. And the proxy is evaluated over several prefixes ending at the token in question, taking the maximum, which is [[prefix-maximization]].

The construction is generic. The paper applies it to Hebrew as well, where the [[hebrew-script-proxy]] correlates $0.55$ with the Hebrew feature.

One acknowledged cost: shared characters like punctuation and whitespace count as non-Arabic, so the proxy misses tokens the feature fires on. The paper lists this first among [[proxy-limitations]].

terms.definition: The probability of observing the string $s$ given that the text is in Arabic script. This is the numerator of the Arabic proxy and the quantity the equation is solving for.
The probability that text is Arabic script given the string $s$. Here it is not learned but assigned by a rule: 1 if every character of $s$ lies in an Arabic Unicode block, $10^{-10}$ otherwise.
The probability of the string under the corpus as a whole, computed as the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities, $P(s) = \prod_{t \in s} p(t)$.
The prior rate of Arabic script in the data, estimated by applying the same Unicode-block character heuristic to a random sample of the dataset.
A string of tokens ending at the token being scored. The proxy is computed over several such prefixes and the maximum is taken.
The identity $P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)$, used here to swap a hard conditional for an easy one in the opposite direction.
A cheaply computable score standing in for "is this string of the hypothesized kind", used as an independent yardstick to compare against a feature's activations.
The form every proxy in the paper takes, $\log(P(s|\text{hypothesis})/P(s))$. The paper's stated reason is that features interact linearly with the logits and so should track log-likelihoods.
A contiguous range of Unicode codepoints assigned to a writing system. Arabic script occupies several, including U+0600–U+06FF and U+0750–U+077F.
The writing system used by Arabic, Farsi, Urdu and other languages. The proxy detects the script, not any one language.
The empirical frequency of each token in the training corpus, treated as independent across positions when forming $P(s)$.

A token that is only part of a multi-byte UTF-8 character, so its script cannot be read off directly. Its script probability is estimated by sampling random occurrences and measuring how often it appears in that script.
The section title flags that Arabic is only the worked example; the same Bayes construction produces proxies for Hebrew and any script with distinctive Unicode blocks.

numbers.meaning: The value assigned to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string consists entirely of characters from Arabic Unicode blocks. It is a certainty by construction, not an estimate: the rule treats an all-Arabic string as definitely Arabic script.

The value assigned to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string contains any character outside the Arabic blocks. It is a tiny probability rather than zero, so the log-likelihood ratio stays finite; the paper notes the proxy is maximized over multiple prefixes, so a heavily penalized prefix simply loses to a cleaner one.
The main Arabic Unicode block, one of the ranges used to decide whether a character counts as Arabic script.
The Arabic Supplement block, a second range included in the same character test. The paper writes "including e.g.", so the list it prints is not exhaustive.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic text, reported in the Arabic feature section. It is the scale of $P(\text{Arabic})$: because the base rate is this low, dividing by it makes a confident Arabic classification produce a large proxy score.

The Pearson correlation between the Arabic feature A/1/3450 and this proxy thresholded at 0, measured over 40 million tokens. It is the paper's headline evidence that the proxy and the feature track the same thing.
The number of tokens over which that correlation was computed.

The Pearson correlation of the Hebrew script proxy — built by the same Bayes construction — with the Hebrew feature A/1/416. Lower than the Arabic figure; the paper attributes part of the gap to a complementary feature that fires on the leading byte token of Hebrew characters.
